claim: Disassembling microtubules can generate movement independently of motor enzymes, especially at kinetochores where they drive chromosome motility.
source: Disassembling microtubules can generate movement independently of motor enzymes, especially at kinetochores where they drive chromosome motility.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about microtubule function, presented as background in the abstract.

claim: In the conformational wave model, protofilaments pull on the kinetochore as they curl outward from a disassembling tip.
source: A popular explanation is the 'conformational wave' model, in which protofilaments pull on the kinetochore as they curl outward from a disassembling tip.
evidence: This describes a theoretical model from the literature.

claim: Curling protofilaments carry ~25% of the energy of GTP hydrolysis as bending strain.
source: Measuring their mechanical work output suggests they carry ~25% of the energy of GTP hydrolysis as bending strain, enabling them to drive movement with efficiency similar to conventional motors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's measurements, as stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Curling protofilaments can drive movement with efficiency similar to conventional motors.
source: Measuring their mechanical work output suggests they carry ~25% of the energy of GTP hydrolysis as bending strain, enabling them to drive movement with efficiency similar to conventional motors.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured work output and comparison to known motor efficiencies.

claim: A β-tubulin mutant (T238V) that dramatically slows disassembly has no effect on work output.
source: Surprisingly, a β-tubulin mutant that dramatically slows disassembly has no effect on work output, indicating an uncoupling of disassembly speed from protofilament strain.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Disassembly speed can be uncoupled from protofilament strain.
source: Surprisingly, a β-tubulin mutant that dramatically slows disassembly has no effect on work output, indicating an uncoupling of disassembly speed from protofilament strain.
evidence: This is inferred from the T238V mutant data showing different disassembly rates but similar work output.

claim: Microtubule polymerization can generate pushing forces.
source: Microtubule polymerization can generate pushing forces (Dogterom and Yurke, 1997; Janson et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microtubule depolymerization can generate pulling forces.
source: depolymerization can generate pulling forces (Coue et al., 1991; Koshland et al., 1988; Lombillo et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Disassembling microtubule tips drive mitotic chromosome movements at kinetochores.
source: An important example of microtubule pulling occurs at kinetochores, where disassembling microtubule tips drive mitotic chromosome movements (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Inoué and Salmon, 1995; McIntosh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism underlying force production by disassembling microtubule tips is unknown.
source: But the mechanism underlying this force production is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Two classes of models have been proposed to explain how disassembling microtubules produce force: conformational wave and biased diffusion.
source: Two classes of models have been proposed to explain how disassembling microtubules produce force, conformational wave and biased diffusion (Koshland et al., 1988; Hill, 1985; Asbury et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Strain energy is trapped after GTP hydrolysis in the microtubule lattice because intrinsically curved GDP-tubulin subunits are held in a straight configuration by their binding to neighboring subunits.
source: Strain energy is trapped after GTP hydrolysis in the microtubule lattice, because intrinsically curved GDP-tubulin subunits are held in a straight (i.e., strained) configuration by their binding to neighboring subunits (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Caplow and Shanks, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stored strain energy is released during tip disassembly when protofilaments curl outward from the tip and break apart, forming a conformational wave.
source: This stored strain energy is released during tip disassembly, when the protofilaments curl outward from the tip and break apart, forming a conformational wave that propagates down the microtubule (Mandelkow et al., 1991; Nogales and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Grishchuk et al. (2005) showed that disassembling microtubule tips can exert brief pulses of force against an attached bead.
source: A seminal study by Grishchuk and co-workers used a laser trap assay to show that disassembling microtubule tips can exert brief pulses of force against an attached bead (Grishchuk et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: The conformational wave might be capable of generating very high forces, up to ~50 pN, according to analysis by Grishchuk et al.
source: Their analysis suggested that the conformational wave might be capable of generating very high forces, up to ~50 pN, but the actual measured forces were much lower (<0.5 pN)
evidence: This is a citation to analysis from a previous study.

claim: Actual measured forces in the Grishchuk et al. study were much lower (<0.5 pN) than the theoretical maximum.
source: Their analysis suggested that the conformational wave might be capable of generating very high forces, up to ~50 pN, but the actual measured forces were much lower (<0.5 pN)
evidence: This is a citation to experimental results from a previous study.

claim: The energy carried by curling protofilaments was not determined in the Grishchuk et al. study.
source: Because of these limitations, the energy carried by the curling protofilaments was not determined.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of previous work.

claim: The work output of the conformational wave mechanism must be limited by the amount of curvature strain energy carried by GDP-protofilaments.
source: Fundamentally, the work output of the conformational wave mechanism must be limited by the amount of curvature strain energy carried by GDP-protofilaments, which dictates how forcefully they can curl outward from the tip.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on physical principles.

claim: Protofilament strain is fundamental to all current models of microtubule dynamic instability.
source: Moreover, protofilament strain is fundamental to all current models of microtubule dynamic instability, and it is generally thought to drive rapid disassembly (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Nogales and Wang, 2006; VanBuren et al., 2005; Molodtsov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Protofilament strain is generally thought to drive rapid disassembly.
source: Moreover, protofilament strain is fundamental to all current models of microtubule dynamic instability, and it is generally thought to drive rapid disassembly (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Nogales and Wang, 2006; VanBuren et al., 2005; Molodtsov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The modified wave assay uses recombinant tubulin with an engineered, flexible tether to minimize interference from the attached bead.
source: Interference from the attached bead was minimized by using recombinant tubulin with an engineered, flexible tether.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: A feedback-controlled laser trap was applied to measure nm-scale displacements as functions of force.
source: By applying a feedback-controlled laser trap, nm-scale displacements were measured as functions of force
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The modified assay enabled direct observation of the spring-like elasticity of curling protofilaments.
source: By applying a feedback-controlled laser trap, nm-scale displacements were measured as functions of force, enabling direct observation of the spring-like elasticity of curling protofilaments
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's measurements.

claim: Curling protofilaments carry a substantial fraction of the energy of GTP hydrolysis in the form of curvature strain.
source: enabling direct observation of the spring-like elasticity of curling protofilaments and showing that they carry a substantial fraction of the energy of GTP hydrolysis in the form of curvature strain.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's measurements.

claim: A 7-fold decrease in disassembly rate had no effect on conformational wave energy.
source: Surprisingly, a 7-fold decrease in disassembly rate had no effect on conformational wave energy, which reveals that the speed of disassembly can be uncoupled from curvature-derived protofilament strain.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the T238V mutant experiments.

claim: Pulses were detected in fewer than half of the trials in the Grishchuk et al. study.
source: However, pulses were detected in fewer than half of the trials, pulse durations varied over 300-fold, and relaxation of the beads into the center of the trap was slower after the trials that failed to produce pulses.
evidence: This is a citation to results from a previous study.

claim: The bead-microtubule attachments in the Grishchuk et al. study restricted outward curling of the protofilaments.
source: These observations suggest that the bead-microtubule attachments, which consisted of multiple biotin-avidin bonds (approximately 3 to 8), restricted outward curling of the protofilaments.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of the previous study.

claim: Pulse amplitudes in the Grishchuk et al. study were probably limited by the maximum distance over which the curling protofilaments could exert force.
source: Moreover, because a fixed trap was used without feedback control, pulse amplitudes were probably limited by the maximum distance over which the curling protofilaments could exert force (i.e., by their working stroke length), rather than by their total capacity for work output.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of the previous study.

claim: Dynamic microtubule extensions were grown from coverslip-anchored seeds assembled from recombinant yeast αβ-tubulin with a His6 tag on the C-terminal tail of β-tubulin.
source: The extensions were assembled from recombinant yeast αβ-tubulin, with a His6 tag engineered onto the C-terminal tail of the β subunit.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Microbeads were tethered to the sides of individual, growing filaments via single anti-His antibodies, creating a strong yet flexible tether (~36 nm in length).
source: Microbeads were tethered to the sides of individual, growing filaments via single anti-His antibodies, creating a strong yet flexible tether (~36 nm in length; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: At low opposing force, a pulse was nearly always observed (90%, or 148 of 164 events recorded at <5 pN).
source: At low opposing force, a pulse was nearly always observed (90%, or 148 of 164 events recorded at <5 pN).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study.

claim: The pulses were large, often >60 nm, which is more than twice the width of the microtubules.
source: The pulses were large, often >60 nm (Figure 1d and e), which is more than twice the width of the microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Disassembling tips can generate pulses of movement more reliably than previously observed.
source: These observations show that disassembling tips can generate pulses of movement more reliably than previously observed.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current results to previous work.

claim: The pulses were fast, with average risetimes between 0.1 and 0.3 s (depending on the level of force), which is 5- to 10-fold faster than in the previous recordings.
source: The pulses were also fast, with average risetimes between 0.1 and 0.3 s (depending on the level of force; Figures 1d,e and 2a–b), which is 5- to 10-fold faster than in the previous recordings.
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The modified tethering scheme imposed less restriction on the outward curling of the protofilaments.
source: These observations suggest that our modified tethering scheme imposed less restriction on the outward curling of the protofilaments.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Pulse amplitudes decreased as the force of the laser trap was increased.
source: Pulse amplitudes decreased as the force of the laser trap was increased (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Curling protofilaments exhibit spring-like elasticity.
source: This behavior demonstrates directly that curling protofilaments exhibit spring-like elasticity.
evidence: This is an inference from the force-displacement measurements.

claim: A 'stall force' was reached at which the pulses were completely suppressed.
source: Eventually a 'stall force' was reached, at which the pulses were completely suppressed (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Depending on bead size, the stall force ranged from 8 to 16 pN.
source: Depending on bead size, the stall force ranged from 8 to 16 pN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The stall force is at least 16-fold higher than the maximal force measured in the previous study (<0.5 pN).
source: which is at least 16-fold higher than the maximal force measured in the previous study (<0.5 pN).
evidence: This is a comparison to results from a previous study.

claim: Protofilaments curling outward from a disassembling microtubule tip behave like springs and can generate forces much higher than previously recorded.
source: In any case, our results show that protofilaments curling outward from a disassembling microtubule tip behave like springs and can generate forces much higher than previously recorded.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study's measurements.

claim: In the lateral push scenario, the curling protofilaments push laterally against the bead at the secondary contact point, causing the bead to pivot about the base of the tether.
source: In the 'lateral push' scenario, the curling protofilaments push laterally against the bead at the secondary contact point, causing the bead to pivot about the base of the tether (Figure 3b).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model for the mechanism, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The predicted leverage in the lateral push scenario is only modest (~2 fold, depending on bead size and tether length).
source: The bead acts as a lever in this case, but because the fulcrum is located at the tether, away from where the curling protofilaments exert their force, the predicted leverage is only modest (~2 fold, depending on bead size and tether length).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the geometric model.

claim: In the axial pull scenario, the microtubule first disassembles past the secondary contact point, allowing the bead to rotate under laser trap tension into an end-on configuration relative to the microtubule tip.
source: In the second scenario, 'axial pull', the microtubule first disassembles past the secondary contact point, allowing the bead to rotate under laser trap tension into an end-on configuration relative to the microtubule tip (Figure 3c).
evidence: This describes an alternative theoretical model for the mechanism, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: There is no leverage in the axial pull scenario.
source: There is no leverage in this case. The unamplified trapping force opposes protofilament curling directly.
evidence: This is a statement about the geometric properties of the axial pull model.

claim: The bead position was nearly always stable prior to the pulses.
source: However, we found that the bead position was nearly always stable prior to the pulses (Figure 1e)
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Only 2% of trials (18 of 760) showed a secondary pulse after the initial pulse.
source: except in a very small fraction of trials (~2%, 18 of 760) during which the initial pulse, from a stable baseline, was followed by bead relaxation toward the trap center and then by a second pulse (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of any relaxation before the primary pulses indicates that these were not preceded by rotation into an end-on configuration, and thus were not generated by axial pulling.
source: However, the lack of any relaxation before the primary pulses indicates that these were not preceded by rotation into an end-on configuration, and thus were not generated by axial pulling.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The lateral push mechanism underlies bead movement in most cases.
source: Thus, it seems that the lateral push mechanism underlies bead movement in most cases.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Larger beads should increase leverage and therefore decrease the amount of laser trap tension required to suppress the pulses.
source: First, larger beads should increase leverage and therefore decrease the amount of laser trap tension required to suppress the pulses.
evidence: This is a prediction from the lateral push model.

claim: Stall forces decreased from 16.2 ± 3.0 pN to 8.4 ± 0.9 pN as bead diameter was increased from 320 to 900 nm.
source: Consistent with this prediction, stall forces decreased from 16.2 ± 3.0 pN to 8.4 ± 0.9 pN as bead diameter was increased from 320 to 900 nm (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Larger beads should produce larger pulse amplitudes when the opposing tension is low enough to allow unhindered movement.
source: The second prediction, also a consequence of leverage, is that larger beads should produce larger pulse amplitudes when the opposing tension is low enough to allow unhindered movement.
evidence: This is a prediction from the lateral push model.

claim: The maximum pulse amplitudes, extrapolated to zero tension, increased from 45.2 ± 3.6 nm to 64.3 ± 3.6 nm as bead diameter was increased from 320 to 900 nm.
source: Indeed, the maximum pulse amplitudes, extrapolated to zero tension, increased from 45.2 ± 3.6 nm to 64.3 ± 3.6 nm as bead diameter was increased from 320 to 900 nm (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The predicted curves for stall force-vs-bead diameter and unloaded amplitude-vs-bead diameter fit the data well.
source: The predicted curves fit our data well, and they are relatively insensitive to the precise tether length (Figure 4a and b)
evidence: This is a comparison of theoretical predictions to experimental data, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The lateral push model provides a good description of the underlying mechanism.
source: suggesting that the lateral push model provides a good description of the underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference from the agreement between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The total work output was independent of bead size.
source: Whereas changes in bead size altered the amplitude-vs-force curve in predictable ways (as discussed above), the total work output was independent of bead size (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The invariance of work output with bead size suggests that W indeed measures the intrinsic strain energy carried by the curling protofilaments.
source: This invariance would not be expected if work output was limited by the attached bead, and therefore it suggests that W indeed measures the intrinsic strain energy carried by the curling protofilaments that pushed against the bead.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation of bead-size independence.

claim: The total work output is estimated at W = 304 ± 24 pN·nm based on a global average across all three bead sizes.
source: Based on a global average across all three bead sizes, we estimate W = 304 ± 24 pN·nm (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The total work output (304 ± 24 pN·nm) is 74-fold greater than thermal energy (kBT).
source: a value 74-fold greater than thermal energy (kBT).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured work output.

claim: A maximum of 4 curls could push simultaneously against the beads.
source: Assuming the lateral push model correctly describes the assay geometry, a maximum of 4 curls could push simultaneously against the beads (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometric model, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The curled segments are ~4 dimers in length.
source: Given the 23° curvature and 8 nm length of an individual tubulin dimer, (Mandelkow et al., 1991; Amos and Klug, 1974) the estimated curl height of h = 20 nm further suggests that the curled segments are ~4 dimers in length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is an inference based on geometric calculations and cited structural data, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total work output may derive from outward curling of as many as 16 tubulin dimers.
source: Thus, the total work output, W, may derive from outward curling of as many as 16 tubulin dimers
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometric model and experimental measurements.

claim: The wave carries at least 19 pN·nm of energy per dimer (4.7 kBT, or 2.7 kcal mole−1).
source: implying that the wave carries at least 19 pN·nm of energy per dimer (4.7 kBT, or 2.7 kcal mole−1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured work output and geometric model, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conformational wave carries considerable strain energy that can be harnessed to perform mechanical work.
source: These observations establish that the conformational wave carries considerable strain energy that can be harnessed to perform mechanical work
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study's measurements.

claim: The study provides a direct estimate of the strain per tubulin subunit.
source: and they provide a direct estimate of the strain per tubulin subunit.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study's measurements.

claim: Mechanical strain in the microtubule lattice is commonly assumed to drive the rapid disassembly of microtubules.
source: Mechanical strain in the microtubule lattice is commonly assumed to drive the rapid disassembly of microtubules, (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Nogales and Wang, 2006; VanBuren et al., 2005; Molodtsov et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a statement about prevailing assumptions in the field, supported by citations.

claim: T238V tubulin forms microtubules that disassemble 7-fold more slowly than wild-type.
source: T238V tubulin forms microtubules that disassemble 7-fold more slowly than wild-type (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conformational wave energy for T238V microtubules was indistinguishable from that of wild-type microtubules.
source: Contrary to this prediction, however, the conformational wave energy for T238V microtubules was indistinguishable from that of wild-type microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study.

claim: T238V microtubules in the wave assay produced pulses that were ~5 fold slower than wild-type.
source: T238V microtubules in the wave assay produced pulses that were ~5 fold slower than wild-type (Figures 4e, 5c,d and 6a)
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: The wave amplitude-vs-force relation for T238V microtubules was essentially identical to that of wild-type.
source: However, the wave amplitude-vs-force relation for T238V microtubules was essentially identical to that of wild-type (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Wild-type and T238V microtubules must store similar amounts of curvature-derived mechanical strain.
source: Thus, even though they disassemble at very different rates, wild-type and T238V microtubules must store similar amounts of curvature-derived mechanical strain (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation of similar work output, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The T238V mutation does not substantially alter the intrinsic curvature, flexural rigidity, or contour length of protofilament curls.
source: The similar amplitude-vs-force curves further suggest that the mutation does not substantially alter the intrinsic curvature, flexural rigidity, or contour length of protofilament curls, because all of these properties together determine pulse amplitude.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation of similar amplitude-vs-force curves.

claim: The mechanical strain energy carried by the dimer was modeled as a function of its bend angle by assuming it behaves as a slender elastic rod with a naturally bent shape, with 23° of curvature when fully relaxed.
source: The mechanical strain energy carried by the dimer was modeled as a function of its bend angle by assuming it behaves as a slender elastic rod with a naturally bent shape, with 23° of curvature when fully relaxed, (Mandelkow et al., 1991)
evidence: This describes the theoretical model developed in the study, based on cited structural data.

claim: The predicted energy landscape implies a curling reaction that proceeds via a high-energy transition state.
source: The predicted landscape implies a curling reaction that proceeds via a high-energy transition state.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical model.

claim: The high-energy transition state should closely resemble the initial, straight conformation.
source: With this assumption, the high-energy transition state should closely resemble the initial, straight conformation (and the curling reaction can be considered 'Eyring-like' [Howard, 2001]).
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical model.

claim: The slower disassembly of T238V microtubules is explained by an increase in the height of the activation barrier.
source: According to this model, the slower disassembly of T238V microtubules is explained by an increase in the height of the activation barrier
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical model.

claim: The data exclude the possibility of a substantially higher transition state energy for T238V because this would lead to a higher wave energy for the mutant, which was not observed.
source: Our data exclude the possibility of a substantially higher transition state energy because this would lead to a higher wave energy for the mutant, which we did not observe.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The T238V mutation specifically strengthens lateral bonds, thereby lowering the energy of the starting state and raising the activation barrier, without altering the intrinsic 23° curvature or the mechanical rigidity of the dimer.
source: We therefore propose that the mutation specifically strengthens lateral bonds, thereby lowering the energy of the starting state and raising the activation barrier, without altering the intrinsic 23° curvature or the mechanical rigidity of the dimer (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and theoretical model, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The lattice of mutant T238V microtubules retained an abnormally high affinity for Bim1-GFP.
source: We observed similar bright Bim1-GFP decoration at the growing plus-ends of mutant T238V microtubules as well, but the lattice of the mutant T238V microtubules retained an abnormally high affinity for Bim1-GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the study, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lattice conformation of T238V tubulin retains structural characteristics that are normally found only near the ends of growing microtubules (GTP-cap-like).
source: This observation indicates that the lattice conformation of T238V tubulin retains structural characteristics that are normally found only near the ends of growing microtubules (GTP-cap-like), which may be associated with stronger lateral bonding in the lattice.
evidence: This is an inference from the Bim1-GFP binding data.

claim: Usually, detaching an end-bound bead by force triggered immediate disassembly of the microtubule (43 of 57 detachments, ~75%).
source: Usually, detaching an end-bound bead by force triggered immediate disassembly of the microtubule (43 of 57 detachments, ~75%), which confirms that tubulin dimers were forcibly removed (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the plucking assay, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: The average force required to pluck tubulins from a wild-type microtubule end was 8.3 ± 0.6 pN.
source: The average force required to pluck tubulins from a wild-type microtubule end was 8.3 ± 0.6 pN (Figure 8d and f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the plucking assay, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Plucking tubulins from mutant T238V microtubules required considerably more force, 19.0 ± 1.6 pN on average.
source: Plucking tubulins from mutant T238V microtubules required considerably more force, 19.0 ± 1.6 pN on average (Figure 8e and f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result from the plucking assay, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: The higher plucking force for T238V is consistent with stronger lateral bonds.
source: This higher plucking force is consistent with stronger lateral bonds, although it could arise from a strengthening of longitudinal bonds, or a strengthening of both kinds of bonds.
evidence: This is an inference from the plucking force measurements.

claim: Mutant T238V tubulin forms relatively stronger tubulin-tubulin bonds compared to wild-type, at least in the context of an assembling end.
source: the observation shows that mutant T238V tubulin forms relatively stronger tubulin-tubulin bonds compared to wild-type, at least in the context of an assembling end.
evidence: This is an inference from the plucking force measurements.

claim: The amount of strain energy carried by curling protofilaments determines the maximum force-generating capacity of the conformational wave mechanism.
source: As with any cantilevered spring, the amount of force that curling protofilaments can produce depends on how they are coupled to the object on which they are pushing (Molodtsov et al., 2005; Efremov et al., 2007). The amount of strain energy they carry is a more fundamental quantity, and therefore less sensitive to geometric details of the coupling. Ultimately, this strain energy determines the maximum force-generating capacity of the conformational wave mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement of physical principles, supported by citations.

claim: Strain energy is fundamentally important for all current models of microtubule dynamic instability.
source: It is also fundamentally important for all current models of microtubule dynamic instability
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical importance of strain energy.

claim: Previous studies have attempted to estimate the magnitude of strain energy using thermodynamic approaches and analyses based on the bending rigidity of intact microtubules, yielding estimates spanning more than an order of magnitude.
source: Thermodynamic approaches (Desai and Mitchison, 1997; Caplow and Shanks, 1996; Howard, 2001) and analyses based on the bending rigidity of intact microtubules (Mickey and Howard, 1995) have yielded estimates spanning more than an order of magnitude (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a summary of previous work, supported by citations and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Previous methods can only infer the stored strain indirectly.
source: But these methods can only infer the stored strain indirectly.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of previous methods.

claim: The wave assay has provided a more direct approach for measuring strain energy.
source: Our wave assay has provided a more direct approach.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The estimated strain energy represents ~22% of the total free energy available from GTP hydrolysis.
source: Our estimate of this stored strain represents ~22% of the total free energy available from GTP hydrolysis (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured work output, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tubulin can convert chemical energy into mechanical work with an efficiency similar to other, more conventional molecular motors, such as kinesin, myosin, and dynein.
source: indicating that tubulin can convert chemical energy into mechanical work with an efficiency similar to other, more conventional molecular motors, such as kinesin, (Howard, 1996) myosin, (Rief et al., 2000) and dynein (Gennerich et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference from the measured efficiency, with citations to motor protein studies for comparison.

claim: The curvature strain energy carried by curling protofilaments is easily sufficient to make a major contribution to the motility of isolated kinetochores and recombinant kinetochore subcomplexes in vitro.
source: The curvature strain energy carried by curling protofilaments is easily sufficient to make a major contribution to the motility of isolated kinetochores and recombinant kinetochore subcomplexes in vitro (Volkov et al., 2013; Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Asbury et al., 2006; Powers et al., 2009; Tien et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the measured strain energy, with citations to kinetochore studies.

claim: The distance moved per released tubulin dimer is δ = 0.61 nm, known from the structure of the microtubule lattice.
source: The distance moved per released tubulin dimer, δ = 0.61 nm, is known from the structure of the microtubule lattice (i.e., the 8 nm length of an αβ-tubulin dimer divided by 13 protofilaments) (Amos and Klug, 1974).
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited structural data.

claim: The maximum force against which a yeast kinetochore has been observed to track in vitro with disassembly is F = 8.5 ± 1.9 pN.
source: The maximum force against which a yeast kinetochore has been observed to track in vitro with disassembly is F = 8.5 ± 1.9 pN (based on a line-fit to tracking speeds measured as a function of tension) (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous experimental result.

claim: The work per released dimer for yeast kinetochores is F·δ = 5.2 ± 1.2 pN·nm (equivalent to 1.3 ± 0.3 kBT per dimer, or 0.74 ± 0.17 kcal mole−1), which is lower than the estimate of curvature strain in the protofilaments by ~3 fold.
source: Multiplying these gives F·δ = 5.2 ± 1.2 pN·nm of work per released dimer (equivalent to 1.3 ± 0.3 kBT per dimer, or 0.74 ± 0.17 kcal mole−1), which is lower than our estimate of curvature strain in the protofilaments, by ~3 fold.
evidence: This is a calculation comparing the study's results to previous kinetochore measurements.

claim: Tip-couplers made by linking recombinant Dam1 complexes at high density to beads via long tethers can sometimes track against forces up to F = 30 pN.
source: Tip-couplers made by linking recombinant Dam1 complexes at high density to beads via long tethers can sometimes track against even higher forces, up to F = 30 pN (Volkov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous experimental result.

claim: The maximum force for Dam1 tip-couplers corresponds to F·δ = 18 pN·nm per released dimer (4.5 kBT per dimer, or 2.6 kcal mole−1), a value nearly equal to the estimated protofilament strain.
source: This maximum force corresponds to F·δ = 18 pN·nm per released dimer (4.5 kBT per dimer, or 2.6 kcal mole−1), a value nearly equal to our estimated protofilament strain.
evidence: This is a calculation comparing the study's results to previous Dam1 measurements.

claim: Nicklas found that the total force required to stall anaphase chromosome movement in grasshopper spermatocytes was 700 pN.
source: The most directly comparable in vivo results are the classic microneedle-based measurements of Nicklas, who found that the total force required to stall anaphase chromosome movement in grasshopper spermatocytes was 700 pN (Nicklas, 1983, 1988).
evidence: This is a citation to a classic in vivo measurement.

claim: Assuming the 700 pN load was shared by 15 kinetochore-attached microtubules leads to an estimate of F ≈ 50 pN per microtubule.
source: Assuming this load was shared by 15 kinetochore-attached microtubules leads to an often-cited estimate of F ≈ 50 pN per microtubule (Nicklas, 1983, 1988).
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited in vivo measurements.

claim: If all the energy driving chromosome movement was derived from disassembly of kinetochore-attached microtubule tips, then the work harnessed per released dimer would be F·δ = 30 pN·nm.
source: If all the energy driving chromosome movement was derived from disassembly of these kinetochore-attached microtubule tips, then the work harnessed per released dimer would be F·δ = 30 pN·nm.
evidence: This is a calculation based on cited in vivo measurements.

claim: The majority of the energy for chromosome movement could be derived from protofilament curvature strain.
source: Our results suggest that the majority of this energy could be derived from protofilament curvature strain.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the study's results to in vivo measurements.

claim: The findings lend strong support to the conformational wave hypothesis for kinetochore motility.
source: By establishing that protofilaments carry enough curvature strain energy to make a major contribution to kinetochore movement, our findings lend strong support to the conformational wave hypothesis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The study reveals how the rate of microtubule disassembly can be altered dramatically by tubulin mutations that do not necessarily affect the amount of lattice strain or the intrinsic protofilament curvature.
source: Our study also reveals how the rate of microtubule disassembly can be altered dramatically by tubulin mutations that do not necessarily affect the amount of lattice strain or the intrinsic protofilament curvature.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the T238V mutant experiments.

claim: The wave assay will be useful for identifying low-strain tubulin mutants and for examining the mechano-chemistry of other recombinant tubulins.
source: We envision that the wave assay developed here will be useful for identifying low-strain tubulin mutants and for examining the mechano-chemistry of other recombinant tubulins.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: The tether linking the bead to the microtubule is approximately 36 nm in length.
source: Adding these values for streptavidin, IgG, and the β-tubulin tail yielded a total of 36 nm for the complete tether.
evidence: This is a calculation based on structural estimates described in the Materials and methods.

claim: The curl height is estimated to be h = 20 nm based on electron micrographs of disassembling tips.
source: given estimates of the height that the curls project from the microtubule surface (~20 nm, based on electron micrographs of disassembling tips) (Mandelkow et al., 1991; McIntosh et al., 2013, 2008)
evidence: This is an estimate based on cited electron microscopy studies.
